items.name: Botai: early horse herders of the northern steppe
items.description: At Botai, a village of pit houses on the Imanburlyq river in northern Kazakhstan, people of the Copper Age hunted, herded and probably rode horses around 3700–3100 BCE: horse bones make up almost all the animal remains, some teeth show wear that may come from bits, and pots hold traces of mare's milk. Ancient DNA (2018) showed that the Botai horses were the ancestors of Przewalski's horses rather than of modern domestic horses, so whether Botai was the first horse domestication is still debated. Dates are approximate (radiocarbon).

items.name: Andronovo: Bronze Age herders and miners
items.description: From about 2000 BCE the Andronovo culture spread across the Kazakh steppe: herders of cattle and sheep who lived in timber houses, buried their dead in kurgans, mined copper and tin in the Kazakh uplands and drove light chariots. They are usually linked with early Indo-Iranian speakers. In central Kazakhstan the later Begazy–Dandybai culture (c. 1300–900 BCE) built monumental stone mausolea. Dates are approximate.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage — Petroglyphs of the Archaeological Landscape of Tanbaly

items.name: The Saka and the Golden Man
items.description: The Iron Age steppe belonged to the Saka, the eastern Scythians of the Persian and Greek sources, nomad warriors who buried their chiefs in great kurgans. The Issyk kurgan near Almaty (4th–3rd century BCE) held the 'Golden Man', a young noble in a coat of some 4,000 gold plaques and a tall headdress; it is now a national symbol of Kazakhstan. Persian kings fought them (Cyrus the Great is said to have died fighting the Massagetae in 530 BCE) and Alexander beat them on the Syr Darya in 329 BCE.

items.name: The Wusun of Zhetysu and the Kangju of the Syr Darya
items.description: Chinese envoys found two great nomad confederations in what is now Kazakhstan. The Wusun took the Ili and Issyk-Kul valleys from the Yuezhi in the 160s–130s BCE and became Han China's allies against the Xiongnu (a Han princess married their ruler around 105 BCE; together they beat the Xiongnu in 71 BCE). Kangju held the middle Syr Darya, the Karatau and the Talas; the rebel Xiongnu chanyu Zhizhi built a fort in their lands, where a Han army killed him in 36 BCE. Both fade from the sources in the 4th–5th centuries.

items.name: Turkic khaganates: the Göktürks, the Turgesh and the Karluks
items.description: The Göktürk (Turkic) Khaganate, founded in 552, took the Kazakh steppe; its western khagans ruled from the Chu and Talas valleys, where the Byzantine envoy Zemarchus met them in 568. After its collapse the Turgesh ruled Zhetysu from Suyab (699–766) and under Suluk (717–738) fought the Arabs in Transoxiana; in 751 the Arabs beat a Tang army on the Talas, ending China's westward push. The Karluks then held Zhetysu from Suyab and Taraz until the Karakhanids (c. 940).

items.name: Oghuz, Kimeks and Kipchaks
items.description: From the 8th century the Oghuz Turks ruled the Aral steppe and the lower Syr Darya from Yangikent; the Seljuks, who conquered Iran and Anatolia, were an Oghuz clan that left around 985. On the Irtysh the Kimek confederation grew up, and in the early 11th century its western wing, the Kipchaks, took over and drove the Oghuz out. From then the steppe from the Irtysh to the Volga was the Dasht-i Qipchaq, the 'Kipchak Steppe'; the western Kipchaks were Europe's Cumans. Kipchak Turkic is the ancestor of modern Kazakh.

items.name: Silk Road towns: Otrar, Taraz, Sayram and the Karakhanids
items.description: Along the Syr Darya and the foot of the Tian Shan ran a chain of walled towns on the Silk Road: Otrar (Farab), Sayram (Isfijab), Taraz, Sauran and Sighnaq, with Talgar and Kayalyk in Zhetysu. Islam came with the Samanids, who took Isfijab and Taraz in the 9th century, and with the Karakhanids, the first Turkic dynasty to convert (mid-10th century), who ruled these towns from Balasagun and Kashgar. The philosopher al-Farabi (c. 870–950) was born near Otrar. The Chang'an–Tianshan corridor sites in Kazakhstan, including Talgar, Aktobe (Stepninskoe), Kulan and Akyrtas, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage — Silk Roads: the Routes Network of Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor

items.name: Ahmad Yasawi and the shrine of Turkestan
items.description: Khoja Ahmad Yasawi (died 1166), a Sufi poet and teacher from the town of Yasi, wrote mystical verse in Turkic and founded the Yasawiyya order, which spread Islam among the steppe nomads. Timur ordered a great mausoleum over his grave in 1389; it was left unfinished at Timur's death in 1405 but is still one of the largest Timurid buildings, and Yasi became known as Turkestan. The Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Kazakh khans were buried there.

items.name: Mongol conquest, the Golden Horde and Moghulistan
items.description: In 1218 the governor of Otrar killed a Mongol trade caravan; Genghis Khan besieged Otrar in 1219 and the steppe was overrun by 1220–22. The north and west became the Golden Horde's eastern wing (the White and Blue Hordes of the sons of Jochi), the south and Zhetysu the Chagatai Khanate. In 1347 its eastern half broke away as Moghulistan, which held Zhetysu and the Ili until the 1510s, while in the west the Shibanid Abu'l-Khayr united the nomadic Uzbeks (1428–1468), took Sighnaq and the Syr Darya towns, and Edigu's heirs founded the Nogai Horde at Saraychik.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Mongol invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire

items.name: The Kazakh Khanate
items.description: Around 1465 the sultans Kerei and Janibek led their followers away from Abu'l-Khayr's khanate to the Chu and Talas valleys; they were called Qazaq, 'free wanderers', and after Abu'l-Khayr's death in 1468 they took over his steppe. Kasym Khan (c. 1511–1521) held Zhetysu and the Syr Darya towns, Haqnazar (1538–1580) beat the Nogai, and Tauekel took Tashkent in 1598. Esim Khan and Tauke Khan (1680–1715, the Zheti Zhargy law code) ruled from Turkestan. The people were organised in three jüz (hordes): the Senior in Zhetysu, the Middle in the central steppe and the Junior in the west. Russia abolished the khans of the Middle (1822) and Junior (1824) jüz; Kenesary Kasymov's revolt (1837–1847) was the last attempt to restore the khanate.

items.name: Wars with the Dzungars: the Years of Great Disaster
items.description: The Oirat Dzungar Khanate, founded in 1634, was the Kazakhs' great enemy for over a century. Its invasion of 1723 drove the Kazakhs from Zhetysu, Turkestan and Tashkent in the 'Aqtaban Shubyryndy' (the barefoot flight), remembered as the Years of Great Disaster. The three jüz joined forces and won at Bulanty (1728) and Anrakay (c. 1730), and the young Ablai made his name in these wars. The Qing destroyed the Dzungars in 1755–1758, and the Kazakhs moved back into Zhetysu and the upper Irtysh.

items.name: Russian protection and conquest
items.description: Abu'l-Khayr, khan of the Junior jüz, swore allegiance to Empress Anna in 1731, hoping for help against the Dzungars; Russia built forts along the Ural, Ishim and Irtysh (Orenburg 1743) and the Middle jüz followed. Ablai Khan (1771–1781) still balanced Russia and Qing China. Russia then abolished the khans (1822–24), took the Senior jüz (1847) and Kokand's Syr Darya forts (Ak-Mechet 1853), founded Verny (Almaty) in 1854, and folded the steppe into its Turkestan and Steppe governorates. Kenesary Kasymov's revolt (1837–1847) and Isatay Taymanov's rising (1836–38) were put down. Russian and Ukrainian peasant settlement took the best pastures.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Russian conquest of Central Asia

items.name: The 1916 revolt and the Alash Autonomy
items.description: In 1916 the Tsar's decree drafting Central Asians for labour behind the front set off a revolt across the steppe and Turkestan; Amangeldy Imanov besieged Turgay, and the reprisals and flight to China killed tens of thousands. After the 1917 revolution Kazakh intellectuals of the Alash party, led by Alikhan Bokeikhanov, declared the Alash Autonomy (December 1917) with its seat at Semey, which sided with the Whites in the civil war until the Bolsheviks took over in 1919–20.

items.name: Soviet Kazakhstan: famine, gulag, Virgin Lands and Baikonur
items.description: The Kirghiz (from 1925 Kazakh) ASSR became the Kazakh SSR in 1936. Forced collectivisation and the seizure of herds caused the famine of 1930–1933 (Asharshylyk), in which about 1.5 million people, around 40% of all Kazakhs, died or fled. Kazakhstan received deported peoples (Koreans, Volga Germans, Chechens) and gulag camps such as Karlag. Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign (from 1954) ploughed the northern steppe; the Baikonur Cosmodrome launched Sputnik (1957) and Gagarin (1961); and the Semipalatinsk test site saw 456 Soviet nuclear tests (1949–1989), closed after the Nevada–Semipalatinsk protest movement. In December 1986 the Jeltoqsan protests in Alma-Ata were crushed.

items.name: Independent Kazakhstan
items.description: Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991, the last Soviet republic to do so. Nursultan Nazarbayev ruled until 2019; the country gave up the nuclear weapons left on its soil, grew rich on oil from Tengiz and Kashagan, and moved its capital from Almaty to Akmola, renamed Astana, in 1997. Police shot striking oil workers at Zhanaozen in 2011. Kassym-Jomart Tokayev became president in 2019; the January 2022 unrest (Qantar), put down with help from Russian-led CSTO troops, ended Nazarbayev's lingering power, and the capital, briefly Nur-Sultan, became Astana again.
